content:
Apple is pushing back against the Department of Justice's attempt to overturn a court ruling that allows Apple to request documents from more than a dozen federal agencies. Here are the details.

Some background

A few weeks ago, Apple won the right to request documents from 14 U.S. agencies as part of its defence in the antitrust case the DOJ filed against it in March 2024.

These include the following agencies and departments:

  • Central Intelligence Agency (CIA)
  • Department of Commerce
  • Department of Homeland Security
  • Department of Defense
  • Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI)
  • Federal Trade Commission (FTC)
  • General Services Administration
  • Department of Labor
  • National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA)
  • National Security Agency (NSA)
  • Office of the Director of National Intelligence
  • Office of Management and Budget
  • Office of Personnel Management
  • Department of State

Apple's argument is that if it can prove that the federal government chose its products for their privacy features, that evidence could support its argument that the practices the DOJ is questioning have legitimate justifications and are not anticompetitive conduct.

After Apple won this dispute, the DOJ promptly filed a motion asking retired federal judge Jose Linares, the special master of discovery in the case, to reconsider his decision.

In complex cases involving large-scale document discovery, courts sometimes appoint special masters to handle narrower disputes, thereby reducing the workload on the presiding judge across the case as a whole. Special masters can be retired judges, practising lawyers, or other experts with relevant experience.

In its motion, the DOJ asked the court to overturn Apple's discovery win, arguing that Judge Linares applied the wrong legal standard by treating those agencies as parties to the case rather than as non-parties entitled to higher discovery protections.

The DOJ also argued that Apple's requests would impose an undue burden on the agencies, citing 13 newly submitted declarations as support, and asserted that the relevance of the documents was limited because federal agencies are not "ordinary consumers."

"This motion fails on every level"

Apple's response to the DOJ's motion is now public, and the company pulls no punches in rebutting each of the DOJ's arguments for trying to overturn the ruling.

Citing several precedents, Apple argues that "the special master's application of the discovery standard to federal agencies as parties was correct," and then dismantles the DOJ's arguments on undue burden and relevance one by one.

Apple said in its conclusion:

Under the schedule Judge Linares set on August 4, no further briefing will be accepted, and it is now up to him to decide whether to uphold the original discovery order or grant the DOJ's request for reconsideration.
